prompt_text: I am preparing an equimolar ethanol + water liquid mixture at 25 °C and atmospheric pressure. What experimental density should I expect?
answer:
{
  "answer": "## Experimental Density of Equimolar Ethanol + Water at 25 °C\n\nFor an equimolar (x(ethanol) ≈ 0.5) liquid mixture of ethanol and water at 298.15 K (25 °C) and near-atmospheric pressure, you should expect a mass density of approximately **859 kg/m³**.\n\nTwo independent experimental sources in the ThermoML database confirm this value:\n\n### Source 1 — DOI: 10.1021/je060335h\n\nMeasured at 101.0 kPa (atmospheric pressure):\n\n| x(ethanol) | T (K) | p (kPa) | ρ (kg/m³) |\n|:----------:|:-----:|:-------:|:---------:|\n| 0.49976    | 298.15 | 101.0   | **858.98** |\n\nNeighbouring compositions at the same temperature and pressure show the composition sensitivity:\n\n| x(ethanol) | ρ (kg/m³) |\n|:----------:|:---------:|\n| 0.47749    | 863.28    |\n| 0.49976    | 858.98    |\n| 0.54464    | 850.55    |\n\n### Source 2 — DOI: 10.1016/j.jct.2018.02.022\n\nMeasured at 92.3 kPa (slightly below standard atmospheric):\n\n| x(ethanol) | T (K) | p (kPa) | ρ (kg/m³) |\n|:----------:|:-----:|:-------:|:---------:|\n| 0.4989     | 298.15 | 92.3    | 860.04    |\n| 0.5002     | 298.15 | 92.3    | **858.963** |\n\n### Consensus\n\nBoth sources agree to within ≈ 0.02 kg/m³ at essentially the same composition:\n\n- **858.98 kg/m³** at x = 0.49976, 101.0 kPa\n- **858.963 kg/m³** at x = 0.5002, 92.3 kPa\n\nThe slight pressure difference (101.0 vs. 92.3 kPa) has negligible effect on liquid density, so these values are directly comparable.\n\n### Chemical Insight\n\nThis measured density of ~859 kg/m³ is significantly lower than what simple ideal (linear) mixing of the pure components would predict. The ethanol–water system is well known for its **negative excess volume**: when ethanol and water are mixed, hydrogen-bonding reorganization causes the mixture to occupy more volume than the sum of the individual pure-liquid volumes. This volume expansion lowers the density below the ideal-mixing estimate.\n\nThe bracketing data also reveal that density changes steeply with composition in this region — roughly −4 to −5 kg/m³ for every 0.01 increase in ethanol mole fraction near x = 0.5 — so precise composition control matters if you need a tight density specification.",
  "core_claims": [
    "The experimental mass density of an equimolar (x(ethanol) ≈ 0.5) liquid mixture of ethanol and water at 298.15 K and near-atmospheric pressure is approximately 859 kg/m³.",
    "Two independent ThermoML sources agree closely: 858.98 kg/m³ at x = 0.49976 and 101.0 kPa (DOI: 10.1021/je060335h), and 858.963 kg/m³ at x = 0.5002 and 92.3 kPa (DOI: 10.1016/j.jct.2018.02.022).",
    "The slight pressure difference (101.0 vs. 92.3 kPa) has negligible effect on liquid density, making the two measurements directly comparable.",
    "The ethanol–water system exhibits negative excess volume due to hydrogen-bonding reorganization, causing the measured density to be lower than an ideal (linear) mixing prediction.",
    "Near x(ethanol) = 0.5, density changes steeply with composition — roughly −4 to −5 kg/m³ for every 0.01 increase in ethanol mole fraction — so precise composition control is important for tight density specifications."
  ],

arguments.instruction: Search for binary mixture data with components benzene and toluene. Filter for temperatures near room temperature (approximately 288-308 K). Report all distinct measured property types (with GLOBprop IDs and names), the mole fraction range covered for each property, the number of data blocks, and associated literature references (GLOBlit IDs and DOIs). Inspect at least one block to show representative data points.

prompt_text: I am deciding whether to validate a liquid-mixture viscosity model first on binary or ternary systems. Which class has enough experimental measurements across composition to provide the stronger test?
answer:
{
  "answer": "## Recommendation: Start with Binary Systems — They Offer the Stronger Initial Validation Test

Based on the dynamic viscosity (Viscosity, Pa·s) data holdings in ThermoML, **binary liquid mixtures** provide the stronger foundation for first-pass model validation, and here is why:

### Data Availability at a Glance

| Metric | Binary (2-component) | Ternary (3-component) |
|---|---|---|
| Distinct literature sources | 1176 | 429 |
| Property blocks | 3294 | 1081 |
| Total data points | 137,229 | 81,066 |
| Avg. data points per block | ~41.7 | ~75.0 |
| Temperature range (K) | 199.918 – 1173.0 | 20.0 – 1023.0 |
| Pressure range (kPa) | 0.0 – 387,800.0 | 0.0 – 196,130.0 |

### Why Binary Systems Win for Initial Validation

1. **Far greater diversity of chemical systems.** With 1176 independent literature sources and 3294 property blocks, binary data cover a much wider variety of solute–solvent pairs — polar + nonpolar, associating + inert, ionic liquids + molecular solvents, etc. This diversity is critical for stress-testing whether a model generalises across chemical families, not just across compositions within one mixture.

2. **Broader thermodynamic conditions.** Binary data span temperatures from ~200 K to 1173 K and pressures up to ~388 MPa, compared with ~20–1023 K and ~196 MPa for ternary data. A model validated over these wider windows is more credible.

3. **Simpler failure diagnosis.** In a binary system the composition variable is one-dimensional (mole fraction x₁), so any systematic deviation between model and experiment can be mapped directly against x₁. In a ternary system, deviations live on a two-dimensional Gibbs triangle, making it harder to isolate whether the error comes from a particular binary interaction parameter or from a higher-order cross term.

4. **Sufficient composition density per block.** Although ternary blocks are denser (~75 points/block vs. ~42), binary blocks still typically sweep 10–20+ mole-fraction values across the full 0 → 1 range at a given temperature — more than enough to reveal curvature, inflection points, or extrema in η(x) that challenge mixing rules.

### When to Move to Ternary Validation

Ternary data become essential in a **second validation stage**, once the model passes binary tests. Ternary viscosity is a much more demanding test of multi-body interaction terms (e.g., the Wohl or Cibulka ternary contribution in excess-property models). The 81,066 ternary data points across 429 sources and 1081 blocks are ample for this purpose, and the higher composition density per block (~75 points) means individual ternary datasets map the Gibbs triangle well.

Notable large datasets for each stage:

- **Binary:** DOI 10.1021/acs.jced.7b00221 (GLOBlit_7152) — 25 blocks, 1448 points; DOI 10.1016/j.jct.2011.02.018 (GLOBlit_3363) — 6 blocks, 848 points.
- **Ternary:** DOI 10.1021/acs.jced.5b00845 (GLOBlit_6743) — 48 blocks, 5168 points; DOI 10.1021/je5001523 (GLOBlit_10411) — 17 blocks, 1604 points.

### Bottom Line

**Binary systems first.** They give you 3× more independent sources, 3× more property blocks, 70% more total data points, wider T/P coverage, and — crucially — far greater chemical diversity, all while keeping failure diagnosis straightforward. Reserve the ternary corpus as the rigorous follow-up test that probes whether your model's multi-component mixing rules hold up in higher-dimensional composition space.",

{
  "answer": "## Ethanol + Water vs. Methanol + Water: Mass Density Data Comparison\n\nFor validating a liquid-density model near room temperature, **ethanol + water is the stronger choice** based on the ThermoML database holdings. It offers substantially more data, broader coverage in temperature and pressure, and denser composition grids at near-ambient conditions. Here is a side-by-side comparison:\n\n### Dataset Size and Coverage\n\n| Feature | Ethanol + Water | Methanol + Water |\n|---|---|---|\n| Data blocks | 29 | ~18 (search-level estimate) |\n| Distinct DOIs | 22 | ~15 (search-level estimate) |\n| Total data points | ~2,920 | ~1,610 (search-level estimate) |\n| Temperature range | 268.1–618.2 K | 287.15–417.15 K (block-verified) |\n| Pressure range | 100–40,000 kPa | 101–29,927 kPa (block-verified) |\n| Composition range | 0–1 (full) | 0–1 (full) |\n\n### Near Room Temperature (298.15 K, atmospheric pressure)\n\n**Ethanol + water** has **54 composition points** at 298.15 K and 100 kPa in a single block alone (GLOBlit_220, PROPblock_2; DOI 10.1016/j.fluid.2004.11.019), with density spanning from 995.3 kg/m³ at x(ethanol) = 0.003 to 785.7 kg/m³ at x(ethanol) = 1.0.\n\n**Methanol + water** has **13 composition points** at 298.15 K and 101 kPa (GLOBlit_2825, PROPblock_10; DOI 10.1016/j.jct.2007.05.004), with density spanning from 787.2 kg/m³ (pure methanol) to 997.05 kg/m³ (pure water).\n\nRepresentative density values at 298.15 K for both systems:\n\n| x(alcohol) ≈ | Ethanol + Water ρ (kg/m³) | Methanol + Water ρ (kg/m³) |\n|---|---|---|\n| 0 (pure water) | 995.3 (at x = 0.003) | 997.05 |\n| ~0.1 | 954.9 (x = 0.1296) | 804.11 (at x(water) = 0.0993, i.e. x(MeOH) ≈ 0.90) — *see note* |\n| ~0.3 | 904.5 (x = 0.3009) | 840.79 (at x(water) = 0.2983, i.e. x(MeOH) ≈ 0.70) |\n| ~0.5 | 859.3 (x = 0.498) | 881.69 (at x(water) = 0.5003, i.e. x(MeOH) ≈ 0.50) |\n| 1.0 (pure alcohol) | 785.7 | 787.2 |\n\n*Note: The methanol + water block reports composition as x(water), so x(methanol) = 1 − x(water). Pure methanol densities are very similar (785.7 vs. 787.2 kg/m³), as expected for these two small alcohols.*\n\n### Why Ethanol + Water Is Preferred for Model Validation\n\n1. **~1.8× more data points** (~2,920 vs. ~1,610), providing better statistical power for parameter fitting and residual analysis.\n\n2. **Broader temperature range** (268.1–618.2 K vs. 287.15–417.15 K verified), spanning from sub-ambient to supercritical-like conditions — a 350 K window versus ~130 K.\n\n3. **Broader pressure range** (100–40,000 kPa vs. 101–29,927 kPa verified), reaching 40 MPa.\n\n4. **Much denser composition grid near room temperature**: 54 mole-fraction points at 298.15 K in a single ethanol + water block versus 13 for methanol + water. This dense grid is critical for capturing the non-linear excess volume behavior that challenges density models.\n\n5. **More independent sources** (22 DOIs vs. ~15), allowing cross-validation between laboratories.\n\n### Chemistry Insight\n\nBoth systems exhibit the classic alcohol–water density behavior: a monotonic decrease from the high density of pure water (~997 kg/m³) to the lower density of the pure alcohol (~786–787 kg/m³). The non-linearity is most pronounced in the water-rich region, where even small additions of alcohol strongly disrupt water's hydrogen-bonding network, producing significant excess volumes. Ethanol, being larger and more hydrophobic than methanol, tends to produce larger excess volume effects, making the ethanol + water system a more demanding (and therefore more informative) test case for liquid density models.\n\n### Recommendation\n\nUse **ethanol + water** as your primary validation system. Report: (1) total number of distinct literature sources (GLOBlit_N), (2) total number of data blocks, (3) number of distinct co-solute compounds paired with water, (4) the temperature and pressure ranges covered, and (5) a representative list of co-solute compounds (up to 10-15) with their GLOBcomp_N IDs.   "answer": "## Activity Coefficient Data for Ethanol + Water: Temperature Range and Key Studies\n\n### Verified Temperature Range\n\nThe ThermoML database contains **6 data blocks** of activity coefficient measurements for the ethanol + water binary system, spanning a verified temperature range of **273.35 K to 372.15 K** across **23 data points** from **4 publications**. All blocks report the **infinite-dilution activity coefficient of ethanol** (γ∞, with mole fraction of ethanol = 0.0).\n\n---\n\n### Coldest Measurement\n\n**273.35 K** — from Vrba, Fenclová et al. (DOI: 10.1016/j.fluid.2005.08.018), PROPblock_4, measured by headspace analysis:\n\n| Temperature (K) | x(ethanol) | γ∞(ethanol) |\n|:---:|:---:|:---:|\n| 273.35 | 0.0 | 2.54 |\n| 283.15 | 0.0 | 3.13 |\n\n### Hottest Measurement\n\n**372.15 K** — from the same publication (DOI: 10.1016/j.fluid.2005.08.018), PROPblock_6, measured by a circulating still method:\n\n| Temperature (K) | x(ethanol) | γ∞(ethanol) |\n|:---:|:---:|:---:|\n| 358.15 | 0.0 | 5.9 |\n| 363.15 | 0.0 | 6.0 |\n| 368.15 | 0.0 | 6.1 |\n| 372.15 | 0.0 | 6.2 |\n\n---\n\n### Complete Block-by-Block Inventory\n\n| Source | DOI | Block | Method | T range (K) | γ∞ range | Points | Trend |\n|---|---|---|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|\n| GLOBlit_299 | 10.1016/j.fluid.2005.08.018 | PROPblock_4 | Headspace analysis | 273.35–283.15 | 2.54–3.13 | 2 | ↑ |\n| GLOBlit_299 | 10.1016/j.fluid.2005.08.018 | PROPblock_5 | Comparative tensimetry | 303.15–333.15 | 4.14–5.3 | 7 | ↑ |\n| GLOBlit_299 | 10.1016/j.fluid.2005.08.018 | PROPblock_6 | Circulating still | 358.15–372.15 | 5.9–6.2 | 4 | ↑ |\n| GLOBlit_8381 | 10.1021/je0495942 | PROPblock_1 | Chromatography | 298.15 | 3.77 | 1 | — |\n| GLOBlit_8511 | 10.1021/je049875+ | PROPblock_1 | Dilutor chromatography | 303.25–343.25 | 5.03–5.96 | 5 | ↑ |\n| GLOBlit_1971 | 10.1016/j.fluid.2016.08.030 | PROPblock_1 | Solid-phase micro-extraction | 323.15–353.15 | 4.11–5.17 | 4 | **↓ (anomalous)** |\n\n---\n\n### Chemistry Insight and Recommendations for Correlation Building\n\n**Consistent data (5 of 6 blocks, 19 points):** In five blocks, γ∞ of ethanol increases monotonically with temperature — physically expected for a system where the hydrophobic interaction between ethanol and water weakens as thermal energy disrupts the hydrogen-bond network. The single most valuable publication is Vrba, Fenclová et al. (DOI: 10.1016/j.fluid.2005.08.018), which alone provides nearly continuous coverage from 273.35 K to 372.15 K using three complementary experimental techniques (headspace analysis, comparative tensimetry, circulating still), contributing 13 of the 19 consistent data points.\n\n**Anomalous dataset — GLOBlit_1971 (DOI: 10.1016/j.fluid.2016.08.030):** This SPME-method dataset shows γ∞ *decreasing* from 5.17 at 323.15 K to 4.11 at 353.15 K, which contradicts every other source. For direct comparison at ~323 K: GLOBlit_1971 reports 5.17, GLOBlit_8511 reports 5.54 (at 323.25 K), and GLOBlit_299 PROPblock_5 reports 5.03 (at 323.15 K). While the absolute values at the lowest temperature are in the same ballpark, the reversed temperature trend is physically suspect and this dataset should be critically evaluated — or excluded — before inclusion in a correlation.\n\n**Practical correlation range:** Your activity-coefficient correlation for ethanol + water can be reliably supported over **273.35 K to 372.15 K** using 19 data points from 3 independent publications with mutually consistent temperature trends.",

arguments.purpose: Find all experimental data for ethanol + water binary system and determine the full temperature range covered, identifying studies with the coldest and hottest measurements
arguments.instruction: Search for the binary system of ethanol (CAS 64-17-5) and water (CAS 7732-18-5). I need to find the widest temperature range of experimental measurements. Look for VLE-related properties: boiling temperature (GLOBprop_14), vapor pressure (GLOBprop_5), and also activity coefficients if available. Screen across all available literature blocks for this binary system. Report the minimum and maximum temperatures found, and identify which literature sources (with DOIs and GLOBlit IDs) provide the coldest and hottest data points.
arguments.context: User is building an activity-coefficient correlation for ethanol+water and needs to know the experimental temperature range available in ThermoML.

answer:
{
  "answer": "## Most Complete Experimental Characterization of Aqueous Propan-2-ol in ThermoML

Based on a search of the ThermoML database covering **71 declared binary data blocks across 38 distinct DOIs** for the water + propan-2-ol system, two studies stand out as the most comprehensive, depending on the criterion used:

---

### 1. Most Property-Diverse Study: GLOBlit_1423 (DOI: 10.1016/j.fluid.2014.02.006)

This study reports **four distinct VLE-related properties** across 4 data blocks and 36 data points:

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| Boiling temperature | Bubble-point temperature at specified pressure |
| Equilibrium mole fraction | Liquid–vapor equilibrium composition |
| Azeotropic temperature | Temperature of the azeotrope |
| Azeotropic composition | Composition at the azeotropic point |

This is the most property-diverse single study for this binary system in the database.

---

### 2. Most Data-Rich Study: GLOBlit_1311 (DOI: 10.1016/j.fluid.2013.08.007)

This study provides the largest dataset with **1,248 data points** across 2 data blocks:

| Property | Data Points |
|----------|-------------|
| Mass density | 1,110 |
| Molar heat capacity (Cp) | 138 |

This extensive coverage of thermophysical properties (density and heat capacity) across multiple temperatures and compositions makes it the most data-rich single study.

---

### Other Notable Studies

| GLOBlit ID | DOI | Property | Points |
|------------|-----|----------|--------|
| GLOBlit_2096 | 10.1016/j.fluid.2017.09.010 | Boiling temperature, Mole fraction, Azeotropic composition | 37 |

| GLOBlit_2892 | 10.1016/j.jct.2007.12.002 | Excess molar enthalpy | 45 |

---

### Measurement Methods and Purities

Unfortunately, detailed metadata on **measurement methods** (e.g., vibrating-tube densimetry, differential scanning calorimetry, ebulliometry) and **compound purities** for these specific studies could not be retrieved within the available query window. The ThermoML database does encode such metadata in its XML records, but the current search was limited to property-level and block-level summaries.

The breadth of properties measured — from VLE and azeotropic data to density, heat capacity, surface tension, excess enthalpy, viscosity, speed of sound, refractive index, and electrical conductivity — reflects the system's relevance to chemical engineering design and thermodynamic modeling.   "answer": "## Estimated Viscosity of Equimolar DMF + Water + Acetonitrile at 298 K\n\n### Direct Measurement: Not Available\n\nNo viscosity data exists in the ThermoML database for the ternary mixture of dimethylformamide (DMF) + water + acetonitrile at 298 K (or any other temperature). However, comprehensive binary viscosity data for all three constituent pairs are available, enabling a well-grounded estimate.\n\n---\n\n### Estimation from Binary Subsystem Data\n\n#### Pure Component Viscosities at 298.15 K (from ThermoML)\n\n| Component | η (Pa·s) | Source |\n|-----------|----------|--------|\n| DMF | 0.0008045 | DOI 10.1021/je300608v (GLOBlit_9900, PROPblock_3) |\n| Water | 0.0008903 | DOI 10.1021/je300608v (GLOBlit_9900, PROPblock_3) |\n| Acetonitrile | 0.0003417 | DOI 10.1016/j.jct.2005.08.009 (GLOBlit_2602, PROPblock_3) |\n\n#### Binary Mixture Viscosities at ~Equimolar Composition, 298.15 K\n\n| Binary pair | Composition | η (Pa·s) | Source |\n|-------------|-------------|----------|--------|\n| DMF + Water | x(water) = 0.5 | 0.0018528 | DOI 10.1021/je300608v (GLOBlit_9900, PROPblock_3) |\n| DMF + Acetonitrile | x(DMF) = 0.5029 | 0.00061 | DOI 10.1021/acs.jced.8b00176 (GLOBlit_7481, PROPblock_18) |\n| Water + Acetonitrile | x(ACN) = 0.5204 | 0.0005387 | DOI 10.1016/j.jct.2005.08.009 (GLOBlit_2602, PROPblock_3) |\n\n---\n\n### Estimation Method: Grunberg–Nissan with Binary Interaction Parameters\n\nThe Grunberg–Nissan equation for a ternary mixture is:\n\n**ln(η_mix) = x₁ ln(η₁) + x₂ ln(η₂) + x₃ ln(η₃) + x₁x₂ G₁₂ + x₁x₃ G₁₃ + x₂x₃ G₂₃**\n\nwhere the binary interaction parameters G_ij capture deviations from ideal (Arrhenius) mixing and are extracted from the measured binary data at equimolar composition:\n\n**G_ij = [ln(η_binary) − x_i ln(η_i) − x_j ln(η_j)] / (x_i · x_j)**\n\n#### Extracted Binary Interaction Parameters\n\n| Pair (i–j) | G_ij | Physical meaning |\n|------------|------|-----------------|\n| DMF–Water (1–2) | **+3.14** | Very strong positive deviation — extensive H-bonding |\n| DMF–Acetonitrile (1–3) | **+0.59** | Weak positive deviation — mild dipolar interactions |\n| Water–Acetonitrile (2–3) | **≈ −0.01** | Essentially ideal — minimal specific interactions |\n\n#### Calculation for x(DMF) = x(Water) = x(ACN) = 1/3\n\n- **Ideal (Arrhenius) contribution:**\n  (1/3) × ln(0.0008045) + (1/3) × ln(0.0008903) + (1/3) × ln(0.0003417) = −7.376\n\n- **Excess (interaction) contribution:**\n  (1/9) × (3.14 + 0.59 − 0.01) = (1/9) × 3.72 = +0.413\n\n- **Total:** ln(η_mix) = −7.376 + 0.413 = **−6.963**\n\n- **η_mix = exp(−6.963) ≈ 0.00095 Pa·s ≈ 0.95 mPa·s**\n\n---\n\n### Result Summary\n\n| Estimate | η (Pa·s) | η (mPa·s) |\n|----------|----------|------------|\n| Ideal Arrhenius (no interactions) | ~0.00063 | ~0.63 |\n| **Grunberg–Nissan (with binary interactions)** | **~0.00095** | **~0.95** |\n\n**Best estimate: η ≈ 0.95 mPa·s (0.00095 Pa·s) at 298.15 K**\n\n---\n\n### Chemical Basis of the Estimate\n\n1. **DMF–Water interaction dominates the excess viscosity.** The DMF + water binary exhibits a dramatic viscosity maximum at x(DMF) ≈ 0.3, reaching 0.0024775 Pa·s — roughly 3× the viscosity of either pure component. This arises from strong hydrogen bonding between water's O–H groups and DMF's carbonyl (C=O) group, which creates structured, long-lived molecular associations that resist flow. The large positive G₁₂ = 3.14 captures this effect. Even at the ternary equimolar composition (where each binary pair is \"diluted\" by the third component), this interaction raises the mixture viscosity well above the ideal prediction.\n\n2. **DMF–Acetonitrile interaction is weak.** Both are aprotic solvents, so no strong hydrogen bonding occurs. The binary viscosity increases nearly monotonically from pure acetonitrile (0.00034 Pa·s) to pure DMF (0.00081 Pa·s) with only a mild positive deviation (G₁₃ ≈ 0.59), attributable to dipole–dipole interactions between DMF (μ ≈ 3.8 D) and acetonitrile (μ ≈ 3.9 D).\n\n3. **Water–Acetonitrile interaction is nearly ideal at equimolar composition.** Although a tiny viscosity maximum (0.0009849 Pa·s) appears at very low acetonitrile content (x_ACN ≈ 0.051), the equimolar binary viscosity (0.0005387 Pa·s) is almost exactly what ideal mixing predicts (G₂₃ ≈ 0). This reflects the well-known microheterogeneity of water–acetonitrile mixtures: at intermediate compositions, the two solvents partially segregate into water-rich and acetonitrile-rich domains rather than forming strong cross-associations.\n\n4. **Net effect in the ternary mixture.** The estimated viscosity of ~0.95 mPa·s is about 50% higher than the ideal Arrhenius prediction (~0.63 mPa·s). The enhancement is almost entirely driven by DMF–water hydrogen bonding. The value falls between the pure water viscosity (0.89 mPa·s) and the DMF–water binary maximum (2.48 mPa·s), which is physically reasonable: the presence of acetonitrile (a low-viscosity, non-hydrogen-bonding diluent) disrupts some of the DMF–water associations, preventing the mixture from reaching the extreme viscosities seen in the DMF–water binary.\n\n### Caveats\n\n- This estimate assumes that ternary interaction terms (x₁x₂x₃ contributions) are negligible. In systems with strong specific interactions like DMF–water, ternary terms can be significant, potentially shifting the result by ±10–20%.\n- The Grunberg–Nissan parameters were extracted at approximately equimolar binary compositions; composition-dependent G_ij values would improve accuracy.\n- No experimental ternary viscosity data exist in ThermoML to validate this estimate.\n\n### Data Sources\n\n| Binary system | DOI | Literature ID | Block |\n|---------------|-----|---------------|-------|\n| DMF + Water | 10.1021/je300608v | GLOBlit_9900 | PROPblock_3 |\n| DMF + Water | 10.1021/je050209y | GLOBlit_8676 | PROPblock_9 |\n| DMF + Acetonitrile | 10.1021/acs.jced.8b00176 | GLOBlit_7481 | PROPblock_18 |\n| DMF + Acetonitrile | 10.1016/j.jct.2014.02.019 | GLOBlit_4124 | PROPblock_6 |\n| Water + Acetonitrile | 10.1016/j.jct.2005.08.009 | GLOBlit_2602 | PROPblock_3 |",

Composition is expressed as mole fraction of water (x_water).   "answer": "## Does the Nonideality of Alcohol + Water Mixtures Grow with Alcohol Chain Length?\n\nThis is a classic question in solution thermodynamics. Using excess molar enthalpy (Hᴱ) as a measure of nonideality, the ThermoML database provides data for two alcohol + water binary systems at 298.15 K and 101.0 kPa, allowing a partial but informative comparison.\n\n---\n\n### Available Data\n\n#### Methanol + Water (DOI: 10.1016/j.tca.2006.02.028, GLOBlit_5688 :: PROPblock_1)\n- **Method:** Titration calorimetry, T = 298.15 K, P = 101.0 kPa\n- Entirely exothermic (negative Hᴱ) across the full composition range\n- **Minimum Hᴱ = −0.850 kJ/mol** at x(methanol) ≈ 0.3\n- Hᴱ at x = 0.5: **−0.777 kJ/mol**\n\n| x(methanol) | Hᴱ (kJ/mol) |\n|:-----------:|:------------:|\n| 0.05 | −0.326 |\n| 0.15 | −0.714 |\n| 0.20 | −0.806 |\n| 0.30 | −0.850 |\n| 0.40 | −0.841 |\n| 0.50 | −0.777 |\n| 0.70 | −0.583 |\n| 0.90 | −0.241 |\n\n#### Ethanol + Water (DOI: 10.1016/j.jct.2005.06.018, GLOBlit_2574 :: PROPblock_4)\n- **Method:** Calvet calorimetry, T = 298.15 K, P = 101.0 kPa\n- Entirely exothermic (negative Hᴱ) across the full composition range\n- **Minimum Hᴱ = −0.77 kJ/mol** at x(ethanol) ≈ 0.15\n- Hᴱ at x = 0.5: **−0.391 kJ/mol**\n\n| x(ethanol) | Hᴱ (kJ/mol) |\n|:----------:|:------------:|\n| 0.0582 | −0.492 |\n| 0.1198 | −0.747 |\n| 0.15 | −0.77 |\n| 0.1837 | −0.767 |\n| 0.25 | −0.702 |\n| 0.2981 | −0.649 |\n| 0.4127 | −0.501 |\n| 0.50 | −0.391 |\n| 0.701 | −0.271 |\n| 0.90 | −0.148 |\n\n#### 1-Propanol + Water and Longer Chains\n**No binary Hᴱ data** for 1-propanol + water (or any longer-chain alcohol + water) were found in the ThermoML database, despite extensive coverage of other properties (density, VLE, heat capacity, etc.) for the 1-propanol + water pair.\n\n---\n\n### Summary Comparison at 298.15 K, 101.0 kPa\n\n| System | Min Hᴱ (kJ/mol) | x(alcohol) at minimum | Hᴱ at x = 0.5 (kJ/mol) | Source |\n|--------|:-----------------:|:---------------------:|:-----------------------:|--------|\n| Methanol + water | −0.850 | ≈ 0.3 | −0.777 | GLOBlit_5688 :: PROPblock_1 |\n| Ethanol + water | −0.77 | ≈ 0.15 | −0.391 | GLOBlit_2574 :: PROPblock_4 |\n| 1-Propanol + water | — | — | — | Not found in database |\n\n---\n\n### Interpretation\n\nThe comparison between methanol and ethanol reveals a nuanced picture:\n\n1. **The minimum Hᴱ values are comparable in magnitude** (−0.850 vs −0.77 kJ/mol), so the *peak* exothermic interaction does not increase dramatically from C₁ to C₂.\n\n2. **The Hᴱ curve becomes markedly more asymmetric with increasing chain length.** The minimum shifts from x ≈ 0.3 (methanol) to x ≈ 0.15 (ethanol) — further toward the water-rich side. This means the strongest enthalpic interactions occur at increasingly dilute alcohol concentrations as the alkyl chain grows.\n\n3. **At equimolar composition (x = 0.5), the nonideality actually *decreases* from methanol to ethanol** (−0.777 vs −0.391 kJ/mol). This reflects the fact that at higher alcohol mole fractions, the longer-chain ethanol disrupts the water hydrogen-bond network so thoroughly that the exothermic contribution from forming alcohol–water hydrogen bonds is diminished.\n\n4. **The growing asymmetry is the key signature of increasing hydrophobic character.** As the alkyl chain lengthens, the hydrophobic moiety increasingly disrupts the cooperative water hydrogen-bond network. At low alcohol concentrations, water can accommodate the solute (hydrophobic hydration), producing strong exothermic effects. At higher concentrations, the water structure is overwhelmed, and the mixing becomes less exothermic.\n\nIn summary, the data available in the ThermoML database show that nonideality in alcohol + water mixtures does evolve with chain length, but in a composition-dependent way: the Hᴱ curve becomes more asymmetric and its minimum shifts to lower alcohol mole fractions. The peak |Hᴱ| values are similar for methanol and ethanol, but the overall shape of the curve changes dramatically, reflecting the growing importance of hydrophobic interactions. A complete chain-length series (including 1-propanol and beyond) could not be constructed from the database, as binary Hᴱ data for 1-propanol + water are not available in ThermoML.",

arguments.purpose: Find excess molar enthalpy (Hᴱ) data for methanol + water binary mixture
arguments.instruction: Search for excess molar enthalpy (GLOBprop_17) data for the binary mixture of methanol + water. Return available data blocks with representative values (especially near equimolar composition x~0.5), temperature conditions, DOIs, and block IDs. Inspect at least one block table to get actual numeric values.
arguments.context: Investigating nonideality trend in alcohol + water mixtures as a function of alcohol chain length. Need Hᴱ data for methanol + water as the shortest chain alcohol.

tool_history.result_full:
<subagent_answer>
{
  "answer": "## Excess Molar Enthalpy (Hᴱ) Data for Methanol + Water Binary Mixture\n\nTwo data blocks of excess molar enthalpy (Hᴱ) measurements were found for the methanol (CH₃OH) + water (H₂O) binary system in the ThermoML database.\n\n---\n\n### Block 1 — Ambient conditions (GLOBlit_5688 :: PROPblock_1)\n**DOI:** 10.1016/j.tca.2006.02.028  \n**Method:** Titration calorimetry  \n**Conditions:** T = 298.15 K, P = 101.0 kPa (fixed)  \n**Data points:** 13 (full composition range, x(methanol) = 0 to 1)  \n**Phase:** Liquid\n\nRepresentative values:\n\n| x(methanol) | Hᴱ (kJ/mol) |\n|---|---|\n| 0 | 0 |\n| 0.05 | −0.326 |\n| 0.15 | −0.714 |\n| 0.20 | −0.806 |\n| 0.30 | −0.850 |\n| 0.40 | −0.841 |\n| 0.50 | −0.777 |\n| 0.70 | −0.583 |\n| 0.90 | −0.241 |\n| 1.0 | 0 |\n\nThe Hᴱ curve is entirely exothermic (negative) with a **minimum of −0.850 kJ/mol near x(methanol) ≈ 0.3**. At equimolar composition (x = 0.5), Hᴱ = **−0.777 kJ/mol**.\n\n---\n\n### Block 2 — Elevated temperature and pressure (GLOBlit_2520 :: PROPblock_3)\n**DOI:** 10.1016/j.jct.2005.03.012  \n**Method:** Flow calorimetry  \n**Conditions:** T = 323.15–514.98 K, P = 2000–10000 kPa  \n**Data points:** 416 (x(methanol) = 0.1–0.9)  \n**Phase:** Liquid  \n**Hᴱ range across all conditions:** −1.1724 to +0.5363 kJ/mol\n\nSelected values at x(methanol) = 0.5, P = 5000 kPa:\n\n| T (K) | Hᴱ (kJ/mol) |\n|---|---|\n| 323.15 | −0.6592 |\n| 325.16 | −0.6406 |\n| 330.50 | −0.6011 |\n| 332.30 | −0.5838 |\n| 348.15 | −0.4457 |\n\nAt elevated temperatures, the exothermic mixing becomes less negative (|Hᴱ| decreases), and at the highest temperatures in this dataset the mixing can even become endothermic (positive Hᴱ values up to +0.5363 kJ/mol are recorded).\n\n---\n\n### Chemistry Insight\n\nMethanol + water is the shortest-chain alcohol–water system. From the ambient-condition data in Block 1 (GLOBlit_5688 :: PROPblock_1, 298.15 K, 101.0 kPa), Hᴱ at x = 0.5 is **−0.777 kJ/mol**, reflecting relatively moderate nonideality driven by disruption and reformation of hydrogen-bond networks. The asymmetric Hᴱ curve (minimum shifted toward the water-rich side at x ≈ 0.3) is characteristic of aqueous alcohol mixtures, where the small methanol molecule integrates relatively well into the water hydrogen-bond network compared to longer-chain alcohols. This value serves as the baseline for comparing the nonideality trend with longer-chain alcohols (ethanol, propanol, etc.), where |Hᴱ| is expected to increase with chain length due to growing hydrophobic interactions.",

answer:
{
  "answer": "## Molar Volume of an Equimolar DMF + Water + Methanol Mixture at 298 K\n\n### Direct Measurement: Not Available\n\nThe ThermoML database contains **no density, molar volume, or excess molar volume data** for the ternary mixture of N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) + water + methanol at 298.15 K or any nearby temperature. The only ternary block found (GLOBlit_5688, DOI: 10.1016/j.tca.2006.02.028) reports enthalpies of solution, not volumetric properties.\n\n### Estimate from Available Binary and Pure-Component Data\n\nHowever, the database provides excellent pure-component and binary density data at 298.15 K that allow a reasonable estimate.\n\n#### Pure-Component Densities at 298.15 K\n\n| Component | ρ (kg/m³) | Source | DOI |\n|-----------|-----------|--------|-----|\n| DMF | 943.81 | GLOBlit_228 / PROPblock_4 | 10.1016/j.fluid.2004.12.004 |\n| Water | 997.06 | GLOBlit_306 / PROPblock_6 | 10.1016/j.fluid.2005.09.009 |\n| Methanol | 786.531 | GLOBlit_57 / PROPblock_1 | 10.1007/s10765-008-0395-z |\n\nUsing standard molar masses (M_DMF = 73.09 g/mol, M_water = 18.015 g/mol, M_methanol = 32.04 g/mol — these are reference values, not database entries), the pure-component molar volumes are:\n\n- V*_DMF = 73.09 / 0.94381 = 77.44 cm³/mol\n- V*_water = 18.015 / 0.99706 = 18.07 cm³/mol\n- V*_methanol = 32.04 / 0.786531 = 40.73 cm³/mol\n\n#### Ideal Mixing Estimate\n\nFor an equimolar mixture (x₁ = x₂ = x₃ = 1/3):\n\n**V_ideal = (1/3)(77.44) + (1/3)(18.07) + (1/3)(40.73) = 45.41 cm³/mol**\n\nThe average molar mass of the mixture is:\n\n**M_mix = (1/3)(73.09 + 18.015 + 32.04) = 41.05 g/mol**\n\nThis corresponds to an ideal mixture density of M_mix/V_ideal = 41.05/45.41 = 0.9040 g/cm³ = **904.0 kg/m³**.\n\n#### Non-Ideal Corrections from Binary Data\n\nThe database provides binary density data for all three subsystems at 298.15 K, which reveal significant non-ideal mixing:\n\n1. **DMF + Water** (GLOBlit_11030 / PROPblock_4, DOI: 10.1021/je700671t): 14 data points. At x_DMF = 0.30, ρ = 991.40 kg/m³; at x_DMF = 0.498, ρ = 976.64 kg/m³. The density plateau near x_DMF = 0–0.10 (ρ ≈ 997 kg/m³) indicates strong **negative excess volumes** (volume contraction) from DMF–water hydrogen bonding.\n\n2. **DMF + Methanol** (GLOBlit_4125 / PROPblock_6, DOI: 10.1016/j.jct.2014.02.021): 26 data points. At x_DMF = 0.5002, ρ = 894.978 kg/m³. Mixing is relatively close to ideal for this pair.\n\n3. **Water + Methanol** (GLOBlit_2825 / PROPblock_10, DOI: 10.1016/j.jct.2007.05.004): 13 data points. At x_water = 0.5003, ρ = 881.69 kg/m³. This system is well known for significant **negative excess volumes** from water–methanol hydrogen bonding.\n\nAll three binary subsystems show densities at equimolar composition that are **higher** than simple linear (ideal) interpolation would predict, meaning all three have negative excess molar volumes (volume contraction upon mixing). The DMF–water pair shows the strongest non-ideality.\n\n#### Best Estimate\n\nSince all three binary subsystems exhibit negative V^E (volume contraction), the ternary mixture will also contract relative to ideal mixing. Typical binary V^E magnitudes for these systems at equimolar composition are on the order of −0.5 to −1.0 cm³/mol. With three such contributions weighted into the ternary, a net excess volume correction of roughly **−0.5 to −1.0 cm³/mol** on the ternary molar volume is reasonable.\n\n**Expected molar volume ≈ 44.4–44.9 cm³/mol** (i.e., the ideal value of ~45.4 cm³/mol reduced by the volume contraction from hydrogen-bonding interactions among all three components).\n\nThis corresponds to an expected mixture density of approximately **914–924 kg/m³**, somewhat higher than the ideal-mixing prediction of ~904 kg/m³.\n\n### Chemical Basis\n\nThe volume contraction arises because DMF is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor (via its C=O group), water is both a donor and acceptor, and methanol is a moderate donor/acceptor. When mixed, these molecules form intermolecular hydrogen bonds that pack more efficiently than the pure liquids, reducing the total volume. The DMF–water interaction is particularly strong, as evidenced by the remarkable density plateau in the binary data where adding DMF to water barely changes the density up to x_DMF ≈ 0.10. This structural effect persists in the ternary mixture and drives the molar volume below the ideal-mixing prediction.",

  "answer": "## DMF Substitutes in Aqueous Mixtures — Viscosity-Characterization Options\n\n### The Baseline: DMF + Water\n\nN,N-Dimethylformamide (DMF) mixed with water is documented in the ThermoML database across **5 independent data blocks**. The most comprehensive dataset (Bernal-García et al., 2008; DOI: 10.1021/je700671t, GLOBlit_11030) contains **98 data points** spanning the full mole-fraction range x(DMF) = 0–1, temperatures 293.15–353.15 K, at 101.0 kPa. The overall viscosity range is **0.000371–0.002954 Pa·s** (0.37–2.95 mPa·s).\n\nAt near-equimolar composition (x(DMF) = 0.498):\n\n| T (K) | Viscosity (Pa·s) |\n|--------|-----------------|\n| 293.15 | 0.002162 |\n| 303.15 | 0.001675 |\n| 313.15 | 0.001337 |\n| 323.15 | 0.001087 |\n| 333.15 | 0.000905 |\n| 343.15 | 0.000764 |\n| 353.15 | 0.000659 |\n\n---\n\n### Option 1: Dimethyl Sulfoxide (DMSO) + Water\n\n**Data availability:** 3 data blocks in ThermoML. The largest (Gracia-Fadrique et al., 2007; DOI: 10.1016/j.jct.2006.12.012, GLOBlit_2781) contains **120 data points** covering x(DMSO) = 0–1, temperatures 298.15–318.15 K, at 101.0 kPa. Overall viscosity range: **0.0005961–0.0037353 Pa·s** (0.60–3.74 mPa·s).\n\nNear-equimolar data:\n\n| T (K) | x(DMSO) | Viscosity (Pa·s) |\n|--------|---------|-----------------|\n| 298.15 | 0.4412 | 0.0036062 |\n| 303.15 | 0.4412 | 0.0032411 |\n| 308.15 | 0.4412 | 0.002876 |\n| 298.15 | 0.5193 | 0.0033124 |\n| 303.15 | 0.5193 | 0.0029921 |\n| 308.15 | 0.5193 | 0.0026712 |\n| 313.15 | 0.5193 | 0.0023483 |\n| 318.15 | 0.5193 | 0.0020253 |\n\n**Why DMSO?** DMSO is the most widely used \"greener\" replacement for DMF. Like DMF, it is fully water-miscible and a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor (via its S=O group). Its aqueous viscosity is **higher** than DMF's at comparable compositions — the maximum viscosity in the inspected block (0.0037353 Pa·s) exceeds DMF's maximum (0.002954 Pa·s). This reflects DMSO's stronger hydrogen-bonding interactions with water. DMSO is less toxic than DMF, biodegradable, and not classified as a reproductive toxicant, making it a preferred substitute in pharmaceutical and fine-chemical applications. The 120-point dataset with 24 unique compositions provides excellent characterization.\n\n---\n\n### Option 2: N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) + Water\n\n**Data availability:** 3 data blocks in ThermoML. The most data-rich inspected block (George & Santhanalakshmi, 2004; DOI: 10.1021/je0340809, GLOBlit_8242) contains **95 data points** covering x(water) = 0.0522–0.99, temperatures 298.15–338.15 K, at 101.3 kPa. Its lactam ring provides a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor (C=O) and a partially exposed nitrogen, creating particularly robust hydration structures. NMP + water shows the **highest viscosities** of the three systems — the maximum (0.005159 Pa·s) is ~1.7× that of DMF + water and ~1.4× that of DMSO + water. This means NMP–water mixtures will behave differently in flow-sensitive applications. NMP's broader temperature coverage (up to 338.15 K) is useful for process design. Like DMSO, NMP is considered less hazardous than DMF, though it does carry some reproductive toxicity concerns at high exposures.\n\n---\n\n### Comparative Summary at ~298 K, Near-Equimolar Composition\n\n| System | x(solvent) | T (K) | Viscosity (Pa·s) | Max viscosity in block (Pa·s) | Data points | T range (K) | Sources |\n|--------|-----------|--------|-----------------|------------------------------|-------------|-------------|---------|\n| DMF + Water | 0.498 | 293.15 | 0.002162 | 0.002954 | 98 | 293.15–353.15 | 5 blocks |\n| DMSO + Water | 0.4412 | 298.15 | 0.0036062 | 0.0037353 | 120 | 298.15–318.15 | 3 blocks |\n| NMP + Water | ~0.50* | 298.15 | 0.003838 | 0.005159 | 95 | 298.15–338.15 | 3 blocks |\n\n*NMP composition reported as x(water) = 0.5018, i.e., x(NMP) ≈ 0.50.\n\n### Key Takeaways\n\n1. **All three systems are well characterized** in ThermoML, with large datasets (95–120 points) covering the full composition range and multiple temperatures.\n\n2. **Viscosity ordering near equimolar composition: NMP > DMSO > DMF.** All three show a pronounced viscosity maximum near x ≈ 0.5, a hallmark of strong hydrogen-bonding interactions between the polar aprotic solvent's carbonyl/sulfinyl group and water.\n\n3. **DMSO is the closest viscosity match to DMF** — its equimolar viscosity (~3.3–3.6 mPa·s at 298 K) is roughly 1.5–1.7× that of DMF (~2.2 mPa·s at 293 K), while NMP is roughly 1.8× DMF. answer:
{
  "answer": "## Non-Ideal Transport Properties of Water + Ethylene Glycol Mixtures\n\nThe water + ethylene glycol (1,2-ethanediol) binary system shows **strongly non-ideal mixing** in its transport properties, and the ThermoML database provides both viscosity and thermodynamic data that quantify and explain this behavior.\n\n---\n\n### 1. Dynamic Viscosity — Large Positive Deviations\n\nFrom **GLOBlit_6951::PROPblock_18** (DOI: 10.1021/acs.jced.6b00526), 33 data points were measured by falling/rolling sphere viscometry at 100.0 kPa across the full composition range.\n\n**Viscosity across composition at 293.15 K:**\n\n| x(water) | Viscosity (Pa·s) |\n|-----------|-----------------|\n| 0 (pure EG) | 0.02113 |\n| 0.2014 | 0.01495 |\n| 0.4011 | 0.01005 |\n| 0.6995 | 0.004584 |\n| 1.0 (pure water) | 0.000949 |\n\n**At 298.15 K:**\n\n| x(water) | Viscosity (Pa·s) |\n|-----------|-----------------|\n| 0 (pure EG) | 0.01724 |\n| 0.2014 | 0.01219 |\n| 0.4011 | 0.00831 |\n| 0.6995 | 0.003884 |\n| 1.0 (pure water) | 0.000843 |\n\n**At 303.15 K:**\n\n| x(water) | Viscosity (Pa·s) |\n|-----------|-----------------|\n| 0 (pure EG) | 0.01423 |\n| 0.2014 | 0.01014 |\n| 0.4969 | 0.005653 |\n| 1.0 (pure water) | 0.000755 |\n\n#### How large is the deviation?\n\nPure ethylene glycol is roughly **22× more viscous** than pure water at 293.15 K (0.02113 vs. 0.000949 Pa·s; ratio derived from the two endpoint values). Under a log-linear (Arrhenius) ideal mixing rule, the viscosity at x(water) = 0.4011 would be approximately 0.006 Pa·s (derived: exp[0.5989 × ln(0.02113) + 0.4011 × ln(0.000949)]). The **measured value is 0.01005 Pa·s** — a substantial **positive deviation of roughly +65%** above the ideal estimate. This means the mixture is significantly more viscous than one would predict from a simple interpolation between the pure-component values.\n\nTemperature strongly reduces viscosity at all compositions: pure EG drops from 0.02113 Pa·s at 293.15 K to 0.01423 Pa·s at 303.15 K — about a 33% decrease over just 10 K (derived from the inspected endpoint values).\n\n---\n\n### 2. Excess Molar Enthalpy — Thermodynamic Confirmation\n\nFrom **GLOBlit_5843::PROPblock_1** (DOI: 10.1016/j.tca.2009.06.004), 13 Calvet calorimetry data points at 298.15 K and 101.0 kPa:\n\n| x(water) | Hᴱ (kJ/mol) |\n|-----------|-------------|\n| 0.1014 | −0.174 |\n| 0.1994 | −0.337 |\n| 0.2091 | −0.347 |\n| 0.3051 | −0.48 |\n| 0.3674 | −0.559 |\n| 0.3995 | −0.59 |\n| 0.4807 | −0.64 |\n| 0.5455 | −0.666 |\n| 0.6144 | −0.698 |\n| 0.669 | **−0.715** |\n| 0.7949 | −0.681 |\n| 0.8656 | −0.57 |\n| 0.915 | −0.423 |\n\nHᴱ is **negative (exothermic) across the entire composition range**, confirming that mixing water and ethylene glycol is energetically favorable. The most exothermic point is **−0.715 kJ/mol at x(water) = 0.669**, corresponding to roughly a **2:1 water-to-EG molar ratio**.\n\n---\n\n### 3. The Chemical Explanation\n\nThe non-ideal transport behavior has a clear molecular origin: **extensive cross-species hydrogen bonding**.\n\n- **Ethylene glycol has two hydroxyl (–OH) groups** on adjacent carbons, making it both a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. Each –OH group can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.\n\n- **The Hᴱ minimum at x(water) ≈ 0.67** (a 2:1 water:EG ratio) is chemically significant — it matches the stoichiometry where each of EG's two –OH groups is optimally solvated by one water molecule. This is the composition of maximum cross-interaction.\n\n- **The asymmetry of the Hᴱ curve** (minimum shifted toward the water-rich side rather than at x = 0.5) directly reflects this 2:1 stoichiometry.\n\n- **Why positive excess viscosity?** When water and EG mix, they form a more extensive and structured hydrogen-bond network than exists in either pure component alone. These cross-linked H-bond clusters resist flow more effectively than the individual pure-component networks, producing viscosities that exceed the ideal mixing prediction. The same favorable interactions that release enthalpy (negative Hᴱ) also create more rigid, cooperative molecular structures that increase viscous drag.\n\n- **Why is the Hᴱ magnitude moderate** (|Hᴱ|_max = 0.715 kJ/mol)? Both pure water and pure ethylene glycol already possess extensive hydrogen-bond networks. Mixing requires **partial disruption** of these existing networks before new, favorable water–EG bonds can form. The observed Hᴱ is the net balance: the energy cost of breaking some water–water and EG–EG bonds is partially offset by the energy released from forming water–EG bonds. The net exotherm confirms that the cross-interactions are thermodynamically preferred, but the magnitude is tempered by the disruption cost.\n\n### Summary\n\nThe water + ethylene glycol system deviates strongly from ideal mixing in its viscosity — measured values exceed log-linear ideal predictions by roughly 65% at intermediate compositions. This positive excess viscosity is driven by the formation of extensive cross-species hydrogen-bond networks, thermodynamically confirmed by uniformly negative excess molar enthalpies peaking at −0.715 kJ/mol near a 2:1 water:EG molar ratio that matches the stoichiometry of EG's two hydroxyl groups.",

arguments.purpose: Find dynamic viscosity data for water + ethylene glycol binary mixtures across composition range
arguments.instruction: Search for dynamic viscosity (GLOBprop_4) data for binary mixtures of water and ethylene glycol (1,2-ethanediol). Return data blocks with composition-dependent viscosity measurements. Include temperature, composition (mole fraction), and viscosity values. Inspect the most relevant block table to show actual data points.
arguments.context: User wants to understand how strongly water + ethylene glycol deviates from ideal mixing in transport properties. Need composition-dependent viscosity data to assess non-ideal behavior.

{
  "answer": "## Dynamic Viscosity Data for Water + Ethylene Glycol Binary Mixtures\n\n### Data Overview\n\nThe ThermoML database contains **7 data blocks** for the water (GLOBcomp_1) + 1,2-ethanediol/ethylene glycol (GLOBcomp_24) binary system with dynamic viscosity (GLOBprop_4) measurements. These blocks span a range of temperatures, compositions, and experimental methods from multiple literature sources.\n\nThe most comprehensive single block covering the full composition range is **GLOBlit_6951::PROPblock_18** (DOI: 10.1021/acs.jced.6b00526), which contains 33 data points measured by the falling/rolling sphere method at a fixed pressure of 100.0 kPa, covering temperatures 293.15–303.15 K and mole fraction of water from 0 to 1.0.\n\n### Composition-Dependent Viscosity Data\n\nFrom **GLOBlit_6951::PROPblock_18** (inspected):\n\n**At 293.15 K:**\n\n| x(water) | Viscosity (Pa·s) |\n|-----------|-----------------|\n| 0 (pure EG) | 0.02113 |\n| 0.2014 | 0.01495 |\n| 0.4011 | 0.01005 |\n| 0.6995 | 0.004584 |\n| 1.0 (pure water) | 0.000949 |\n\n**At 298.15 K:**\n\n| x(water) | Viscosity (Pa·s) |\n|-----------|-----------------|\n| 0 (pure EG) | 0.01724 |\n| 0.2014 | 0.01219 |\n| 0.4011 | 0.00831 |\n| 0.6995 | 0.003884 |\n| 1.0 (pure water) | 0.000843 |\n\n**At 303.15 K:**\n\n| x(water) | Viscosity (Pa·s) |\n|-----------|-----------------|\n| 0 (pure EG) | 0.01423 |\n| 0.2014 | 0.01014 |\n| 0.4969 | 0.005653 |\n| 1.0 (pure water) | 0.000755 |\n\nOverall stats for this block: viscosity ranges from **0.000755 to 0.02113 Pa·s** across all 33 data points.\n\n### Non-Ideal Mixing Behavior\n\nThe data reveal **strongly non-ideal mixing** in the viscosity of this system:\n\n- Pure ethylene glycol is **far more viscous** than pure water at 293.15 K (0.02113 vs. 0.000949 Pa·s — a ratio of approximately 0.02113 ÷ 0.000949 ≈ 22, derived by dividing the two inspected endpoint values).\n- The composition dependence is highly nonlinear. Under a simple log-linear (Arrhenius) ideal mixing rule at 293.15 K, the estimated viscosity at x(water) = 0.4011 would be approximately 0.006 Pa·s (derived calculation: exp((1 − 0.4011) × ln(0.02113) + 0.4011 × ln(0.000949)), where 1 − 0.4011 = 0.5989 is the complementary EG mole fraction), but the measured value is **0.01005 Pa·s** — a substantial **positive deviation** (derived comparison: the measured value is roughly 65% higher than the log-linear ideal estimate).\n- This positive excess viscosity is characteristic of systems with strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding between the two components. Water and ethylene glycol form extensive H-bond networks, with EG acting as both donor and acceptor through its two hydroxyl groups, creating more structured and viscous mixtures than ideal mixing would predict.\n- Temperature strongly reduces viscosity across all compositions, with pure EG viscosity dropping from 0.02113 Pa·s at 293.15 K to 0.01423 Pa·s at 303.15 K (a ~33% decrease over just 10 K; derived from inspected values).\n\nThis system is a textbook example of how hydrogen-bonding interactions between unlike molecules can produce transport-property deviations well beyond what thermodynamic excess Gibbs energy alone would suggest.\n\n---\n[UNGROUNDED DATA FLAGS] The following quoted values could not be verified against any verbatim data inspection in this run and must be treated as UNVERIFIED:\n- **UNGROUNDED_LITERAL** GLOBlit_6951::PROPblock_18: 22 (near '…000949 Pa·s — a ratio of approximately 0.02113 ÷ 0.000949 ≈ …') matches no inspected row/stat, database table, or other source of GLOBlit_6951::PROPblock_18\n  fix (ONLY if this is meant to be a database datum): `inspect_block_table(block_number=\"GLOBlit_6951::PROPblock_18\", nearest={\"column\": \"temperature_k\", \"value\": 22.0})` — if it is a value you computed or an external reference, keep it and label its provenance instead\n- **UNGROUNDED_LITERAL** GLOBlit_6951::PROPblock_18: 0.5989 (near '…× ln(0.02113) + 0.4011 × ln(0.000949)), where 1 - 0.4011 = 0…') matches no inspected row/stat, database table, or other source of GLOBlit_6951::PROPblock_18\n  fix (ONLY if this is meant to be a database datum): `inspect_block_table(block_number=\"GLOBlit_6951::PROPblock_18\", nearest={\"column\": \"temperature_k\", \"value\": 0.5989})` — if it is a value you computed or an external reference, keep it and label its provenance instead\nInspected so far: PROPblock_18",

{
  "answer": "## How Viscosity Changes with the Molecular Structure of the Organic Component in Aqueous Mixtures\n\n### Overview\n\nData from the ThermoML database for four binary alcohol–water systems at 298.15 K and 101 kPa reveal clear, systematic trends linking the molecular structure of the organic component to the viscosity behaviour of the aqueous mixture. The key structural variables explored are **alkyl chain length** (methanol → ethanol → 1-propanol) and **chain branching** (1-propanol vs. 2-propanol).\n\nAll data were measured by capillary tube (Ubbelohde) viscometry and come from two internally consistent studies:\n- DOI 10.1016/j.jct.2007.05.004 (methanol + water, ethanol + water)\n- DOI 10.1021/je700700f (1-propanol + water, 2-propanol + water)\n\n---\n\n### 1. The Universal Viscosity Maximum\n\nEvery alcohol–water system examined displays a **non-monotonic viscosity profile**: starting from pure water (η = 0.00089 Pa·s), viscosity rises with increasing alcohol content, passes through a pronounced maximum at an intermediate composition, and then decreases toward the pure alcohol value. This maximum is the signature of strong, composition-dependent intermolecular interactions in the mixture.\n\n---\n\n### 2. Effect of Alkyl Chain Length\n\n#### Pure-component viscosities at 298.15 K\n\n| Compound | η (Pa·s) | Source |\n|----------|----------|--------|\n| Water | 0.00089 | All blocks |\n| Methanol (C₁) | 0.000545 | PROPblock_9 |\n| Ethanol (C₂) | 0.001082 | PROPblock_11 |\n| 1-Propanol (C₃) | 0.002017 | PROPblock_12 |\n| 2-Propanol (C₃, branched) | 0.002082 | PROPblock_15 |\n\nPure alcohol viscosity increases steadily with chain length (0.000545 → 0.001082 → 0.002017 Pa·s for C₁–C₃), reflecting stronger London dispersion forces and more extensive van der Waals contact area as the hydrocarbon portion grows.\n\n#### Peak mixture viscosities at 298.15 K\n\n| Alcohol | Peak η (Pa·s) | x(alcohol) at peak | Ratio peak/water |\n|---------|---------------|---------------------|------------------|\n| Methanol | 0.001554 | ~0.30 | 1.75× |\n| Ethanol | 0.0023 | ~0.20 | 2.58× |\n| 1-Propanol | 0.002691 | ~0.30 | 3.02× |\n| 2-Propanol | 0.003087 | ~0.30 | 3.47× |\n\n**Key trend:** The peak viscosity increases dramatically with chain length — methanol (0.001554) < ethanol (0.0023) < 1-propanol (0.002691 Pa·s). Longer alkyl chains amplify the viscosity enhancement by a factor of nearly 2 from C₁ to C₃.\n\n---\n\n### 3. Effect of Chain Branching (1-Propanol vs. 2-Propanol)\n\nBoth propanol isomers (C₃H₈O) share the same molecular formula and similar pure-component viscosities (0.002017 vs. 0.002082 Pa·s), yet the branched isomer (2-propanol) produces a **~15% higher peak viscosity** in aqueous mixtures (0.003087 vs. 0.002691 Pa·s), with both peaks occurring near x(alcohol) ≈ 0.30. This comparison is especially robust because both datasets come from the same laboratory, method, and conditions.\n\n---\n\n### 4. Representative Data\n\n#### Methanol + Water (PROPblock_9, DOI 10.1016/j.jct.2007.05.004)\n\n| x(methanol) | η (Pa·s) |\n|-------------|----------|\n| 0 (pure water) | 0.00089 |\n| 0.1007 | 0.000677 |\n| 0.3003 | 0.001554 ← peak |\n| 0.5006 | 0.001463 |\n| 1.0 (pure MeOH) | 0.000545 |\n\n*(Composition expressed as x(water) in the source; converted here: x(methanol) = 1 − x(water))*\n\n#### Ethanol + Water (PROPblock_11, DOI 10.1016/j.jct.2007.05.004)\n\n| x(ethanol) | η (Pa·s) |\n|------------|----------|\n| 0 (pure water) | 0.00089 |\n| 0.1004 | 0.00186 |\n| 0.1999 | 0.0023 ← peak |\n| 0.4011 | 0.002115 |\n| 1.0 (pure EtOH) | 0.001082 |\n\n#### 1-Propanol + Water (PROPblock_12, DOI 10.1021/je700700f)\n\n| x(1-propanol) | η (Pa·s) |\n|---------------|----------|\n| 0 | 0.00089 |\n| 0.0504 | 0.001616 |\n| 0.0993 | 0.002121 |\n| 0.2979 | 0.002691 ← peak |\n| 0.4955 | 0.002494 |\n| 1.0 | 0.002017 |\n\n#### 2-Propanol + Water (PROPblock_15, DOI 10.1021/je700700f)\n\n| x(2-propanol) | η (Pa·s) |\n|---------------|----------|\n| 0 | 0.00089 |\n| 0.0491 | 0.001718 |\n| 0.1008 | 0.002495 |\n| 0.2994 | 0.003087 ← peak |\n| 0.3992 | 0.002924 |\n| 1.0 | 0.002082 |\n\n---\n\n### 5. Intermolecular Interactions Explaining the Trends\n\nThe viscosity behaviour of aqueous alcohol mixtures is governed by a competition among several intermolecular interactions:\n\n#### (a) Hydrogen bonding (H-bonding)\nBoth water and alcohols are strong hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. In mixtures, **cross-associated water–alcohol hydrogen bonds** form cooperatively, creating transient, extended networks that are more structured than either pure liquid alone. This cooperative H-bonding is the primary origin of the viscosity maximum: at intermediate compositions, the density of cross-associated H-bonds is highest, producing maximum resistance to flow.\n\n#### (b) Hydrophobic hydration\nWater molecules reorganize around the non-polar alkyl portion of the alcohol to form ordered, cage-like \"iceberg\" structures (Frank–Evans hydrophobic hydration). These structured hydration shells:\n- Increase the effective hydrodynamic volume of the solute\n- Slow molecular rearrangement and momentum transfer\n- Become more extensive as the alkyl chain lengthens, explaining why the peak viscosity grows from methanol (C₁) to 1-propanol (C₃)\n\nThe data quantify this: the peak viscosity rises from 0.001554 Pa·s (methanol) to 0.002691 Pa·s (1-propanol), a 73% increase for adding just two –CH₂– groups.\n\n#### (c) Hydrophobic association\nAt higher alcohol concentrations, alcohol molecules begin to self-aggregate through hydrophobic interactions, partially disrupting the water network. This causes the viscosity to decrease beyond the peak composition, eventually approaching the pure alcohol value.\n\n#### (d) Molecular geometry and branching effects\nThe comparison of 1-propanol and 2-propanol — same molecular formula, same number of H-bond sites — isolates the effect of molecular shape. The branched 2-propanol produces a higher peak viscosity (0.003087 vs. 0.002691 Pa·s). This can be attributed to:\n- **More compact molecular geometry** → the branched molecule presents a larger effective cross-section to the surrounding water cage, requiring more water molecules to complete the hydration shell\n- **Tighter packing of hydration structures** → the isopropyl group's globular shape may template more ordered water cages compared to the elongated n-propyl chain\n- **Reduced rotational freedom** → branching restricts internal rotation, making the hydrated complex more rigid and increasing its contribution to viscosity\n\n#### (e) Composition of the peak\nThe peak shifts to lower alcohol mole fractions as the alkyl chain grows: ~0.30 for methanol, ~0.20 for ethanol, and ~0.30 for both propanols. For ethanol, the shift to lower x(alcohol) reflects the fact that each larger alcohol molecule disrupts a greater volume of water structure, so the maximum cooperative H-bonding network is achieved at a lower alcohol mole fraction.\n\n---\n\n### 6. Summary of Structure–Viscosity Relationships\n\n| Structural change | Effect on peak mixture viscosity | Primary interaction responsible |\n|---|---|---|\n| Increasing chain length (C₁→C₂→C₃) | Increases: 0.001554 → 0.0023 → 0.002691 Pa·s | Enhanced hydrophobic hydration; larger non-polar surface |\n| Branching (n-C₃ → iso-C₃) | Increases: 0.002691 → 0.003087 Pa·s (+15%) | More compact geometry → tighter hydration shell packing |\n| Adding –OH group (alcohol vs. water) | Creates viscosity maximum above either pure component | Cooperative cross-associated H-bonding |\n\nThese data demonstrate that in aqueous mixtures of organic solvents, viscosity is not simply additive — it is governed by the interplay of hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic hydration, and molecular geometry, all of which are systematically modulated by the structure of the organic component.",

arguments.purpose: Find viscosity data for aqueous mixtures of small alcohols (methanol, ethanol, 1-propanol, 2-propanol) to compare how alcohol chain length and branching affect mixture viscosity
arguments.instruction: Search for dynamic viscosity (GLOBprop_4) data in binary aqueous mixtures containing methanol, ethanol, 1-propanol, or 2-propanol. The inspected values are highly consistent:\n\n### Inspected Data Points at 298.15 K\n\n| Source (DOI) | Literature | Block | T (K) | P (kPa) | ρ (kg/m³) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 10.1007/s10765-008-0395-z | GLOBlit_57 | PROPblock_7 | 298.15 | 101.325 | 1095.271 |\n| 10.1007/s10765-009-0648-5 | GLOBlit_86 | PROPblock_4 | 298.15 | 101.0 | 1095.278 |\n| 10.1016/j.fluid.2010.01.002 | GLOBlit_779 | PROPblock_3 | 298.15 | 101.325 | 1095.27 |\n| 10.1016/j.fluid.2011.02.010 | GLOBlit_938 | PROPblock_3 | 298.15 | 101.0 | 1095.37 |\n| 10.1016/j.fluid.2013.05.001 | GLOBlit_1246 | PROPblock_1 | 298.15 | 85.9 | 1095.29 |\n\n### Temperature Dependence (GLOBlit_86, PROPblock_4)\n\nThe GLOBlit_86 block provides a temperature series showing the density decreases monotonically and nearly linearly with temperature:\n\n| BLKpoint_id | T (K) | P (kPa) | ρ (kg/m³) |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| BLKpoint_2 | 293.15 | 101.0 | 1100.306 |\n| BLKpoint_3 | 298.15 | 101.0 | 1095.278 |\n| BLKpoint_4 | 303.15 | 101.0 | 1090.253 |\n\nThe full block spans 288.15–308.15 K with density ranging from 1085.231 to 1105.336 kg/m³ (5 data points).\n\n### Summary\n\nThe mass density of pure liquid DMSO at 298.15 K and near-atmospheric pressure is consistently reported across five inspected sources in the narrow range **1095.27–1095.37 kg/m³** (equivalently ~1.0953 g/cm³). The slight variation (< 0.1 kg/m³ among four sources, with GLOBlit_938 at 1095.37 kg/m³ being the highest) likely reflects minor differences in sample purity and pressure conditions. The temperature coefficient near 298.15 K is approximately −1.0 kg·m⁻³·K⁻¹, as seen from the GLOBlit_86 data where density drops from 1100.306 kg/m³ at 293.15 K to 1090.253 kg/m³ at 303.15 K.\n\nNote: GLOBlit_1775::PROPblock_6 was not inspected in this run due to the iteration limit, so its data value is not quoted here.",
